knowledge_point.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Substitution

question.:question/worked-solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =2 x^{4} + 9 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =8 x^{3} \\ \text{d}u & =8 x^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}u & =x^{3}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=2 x^{4} + 9.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & -1 & 0 \\ u & 11 & 9\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\int_{-1}^{0}\frac{2 x^{3}}{2 x^{4} + 9}\,\text{d}x=\int_{11}^{9}\frac{2}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{11}^{9}\frac{2}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}\int_{11}^{9}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\ln(u)|_{11}^{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\ln(9)-\ln(11)) \\  & =- \frac{\log{\left(11 \right)}}{4} + \frac{\log{\left(3 \right)}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
